content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Heaven is primarily the transcendent dwelling place of God — his throne, presence, and rule — and, derivatively, the eternal destiny/home of the redeemed who will enjoy unbroken fellowship with him. Secondary senses include the physical sky, 'kingdom of heaven' as God's reign, an intermediate state, and (as a listed common alternative) the new-creation view that the final hope is heaven united with a renewed earth rather than souls going up to heaven.","book_summary":"Heaven is the jurisdiction where God's will is already done — sky and seat of rule fused in the single dual word shamayim — set over against earth, the delegated realm of men where his will must yet be done. The characteristic motion is downward (rain, fire, the Son, the New Jerusalem); ascent is Babel's error. The hope is heaven come down to earth, not man gone up to heaven.","consensus_core_identification":"God's transcendent dwelling/throne-realm, and the redeemed's eternal home with him.","book_core_identification":"The realm of God's accomplished rule (throne + sky in one word), whose relation to earth is jurisdictional and whose eschatological movement is exclusively descent to earth, not human ascent.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains heaven as God's throne-realm but excludes or reframes the widespread derivative sense of heaven as the destination believers go up to. It reclassifies the redeemed's hope: not residence attained by ascent, but heaven's descent to a renewed earth ('heaven come down, not man gone up'), and it brands upward aspiration as Babel. It also insists the sky-sense and throne-sense are one dual word rather than separable meanings, and adds a 'jurisdiction where God's will is already done' framing keyed to Matt 6:10 and Ps 115:16 that the consensus statements do not foreground.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book's central referent is still the consensus referent — the realm of God's presence, throne, and rule (Isa 66:1 cited by both). So the core is not replaced. But the book materially tightens the boundary: it rejects the consensus's derivative identification of heaven as the place the redeemed go up to, replacing it with a descent-only eschatology. This move is anticipated in the consensus itself: Responses A and C explicitly list the new-heavens-and-new-earth / New-Jerusalem-descends view (N. T. Wright-style) as a common alternative, so the book's position is a sharpened selection within the recognized field, not a novel or contradictory identification. Its distinctive 'jurisdiction of accomplished will' and anti-Babel framing adds precision and polemical edge rather than a new referent. Hence REFINED with BOOK_NARROWS at the core and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION of the covered cases (the believer's hope is reclassified from ascent-destination to descended dwelling).","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the book's descent emphasis is already listed as a common consensus alternative, and its throne/rule core matches the consensus primary, so the difference is emphasis rather than material boundary change. Against this, the consensus primary across all four responses explicitly includes heaven as the redeemed's eternal home/destiny, which the book pointedly recasts ('not man gone up'), making the disagreement more than wording.","confidence":"high"}
